note: Authored ground truth for CORPUS.md §2.14(a). Five documents, five roles. The unit list is what a correct extractor should find, written before the extractor existed.

units.text: A batch must be acknowledged within two seconds.
A batch is committed whole or not at all; partial ingestion never occurs.
Rejected batches remain retrievable for thirty days.
Operators can replay any accepted batch without engineering involvement.
Ingestion is queue-backed; batches are acknowledged before processing.
units.rationale: Synchronous validation cannot meet the acknowledgement budget under load.

units.text: Schemas are declared by the customer, never inferred.
units.rationale: Inference was the dominant incident source in the previous system.

units.text: Modules are named for what they do, not for the pattern they use.
Never swallow an error to keep a request alive.
Every bug fix ships with the test that would have caught it.
A new runtime dependency requires a written reason in the pull request.
Do not delete queued batches; they are the only copy until the warehouse commit succeeds.

retiredNearDuplicates.why: Asserted as the same latency constraint stated in a PRD and in an ADR. It is not: a p95 engineering budget is not a per-user ceiling, and merging drops `more` and `second`. Jaccard 0.000, so the lexical claim held; the identity claim did not.

a.text: No user should ever wait more than two seconds for a batch to be acknowledged.

b.text: The p95 acknowledgement budget for a single submission is 2000 milliseconds.

retiredNearDuplicates.why: Asserted as whole-batch atomicity stated twice. It is not: a rule about what happens on validation failure is not the rule about commit atomicity, and merging drops `whole`. The second implies the first only if you already believe they are the same design, which is the assumption the corpus was encoding.

a.text: A batch that fails validation must be rejected whole. Partial ingestion is never acceptable.

b.text: A submission is committed in one transaction or not at all.

mustNotMerge.why: The hardest of the four, and the one nothing structural catches: two sequential steps of one procedure. Same category, and the SAME entityKey, because both sit under the runbook's `## Deploy` heading — so entity blocking does not apply and the adjudicator has to reject them on meaning alone. A method that merges these collapses a deploy procedure into one step.

Measured cosine 0.7428 against nomic-embed-text-v1.5 — above BOTH authored near-duplicate pairs (0.63, 0.62). Same category, neither carries an entityKey, so this too reaches the model. One is about when a batch is rejected, the other about how long a rejected batch is kept: adjacent subject, different facts.

a.text: Every rejected batch must be retrievable for thirty days.

b.text: A batch that fails validation must be rejected whole.

mustNotMerge.why: Measured cosine 0.8201 — the highest-scoring pair in the entire clean set, higher than either true near-duplicate. A timeout and a size cap are maximally topical and completely different facts. Caught structurally, by differing entityKeys, which is recorded here as a REQUIREMENT rather than left as an accident of implementation: remove that block and the highest-cosine pair in the corpus merges.
Both concern what an operator may do with a batch after ingestion, in the same document and the same category, and they are independent requirements — one could be met while the other is violated.

a.text: Operators must be able to replay any accepted batch without contacting engineering.

b.text: Every rejected batch must be retrievable for thirty days.
